title: An approximate dynamic programming approach to multidimensional knapsack problems
contribution: An ADP framework for the multidimensional knapsack problem that uses a base heuristic (best: a new LP-based adaptive-fixing heuristic) as the cost-to-go estimate; on random and literature instances it reaches near-LP-bound quality about 75 times faster than CPLEX 6.0 at matched quality and much faster than a genetic algorithm of slightly better quality, while parametric and nonparametric value approximations are reported not competitive (pp. 1, 11-15).
problem_entry: Method-first (IO+HS): tests whether ADP, successful mainly on stochastic problems, is a realistic alternative for large deterministic MKPs, judged by speed, quality and robustness (p. 2); the MKP is motivated by applications and the set-cover reduction (pp. 1, 3); exact DP needs O(n b*^m) work (p. 3).
key_idea: DP over items and residual capacity (pp. 2-3) with the value function replaced by (a) a base heuristic's value rescaled to a common percentage gap below the truncated LP bound, plus reduced-cost fixing, early termination and lag fixing (ADP-BH, pp. 3-5); (b) a stagewise linear fit motivated by probabilistic asymptotics (ADP-P, p. 7); (c) kernel interpolation over sampled states (ADP-N, p. 8); new base heuristic: LP adaptive fixing with threshold delta (p. 6).
assumptions: MKP with nonnegative data (p. 2); random uncorrelated, weakly and strongly correlated instances, 10 per class and size, b = 0.5 sum a_ij, up to m = 100, n = 1000 (p. 9); Chu-Beasley's largest instances (p. 11); ADP-P rests on i.i.d. columns with b = n*beta, under which Z_LP/n and Z_MKP/n share a limit (p. 7); uniform state sample kept after stratified and random samples did no better (p. 7).
proof_devices: DP recursion (3)-(4) and complexity count O(n b*^m) (p. 3)
Reduced-cost fixing with the heuristic value as the incumbent bound, citing Nemhauser-Wolsey (p. 4)
Both branch estimates scaled to the same percentage gap below the truncated LP bound, (1 - delta*)U (p. 4)
Subproblem optimality tests when the heuristic value equals the LP upper bound (pp. 4-5)
Least-absolute-deviation fit rewritten as an LP and solved with CPLEX (p. 7)
Kernel regression over a uniform state sample with a Fan-Gijbels kernel (p. 8)
No approximation guarantee for any ADP variant; the only theory is imported probabilistic asymptotics (p. 7)
experiments: Dell Precision 410 under Linux; instances posted online (p. 9); quality = % deviation from the LP value (p. 9); adaptive fixing best of six heuristics (PE 1.14/1.81/2.49, p. 10); ADP-H2 PE 0.68/1.11/1.51, about 30% better than H2 (p. 11); vs the Chu-Beasley GA on its own instances with GA times halved for machine speed: GA PE 0.56 vs 0.74-0.80 but 1,287.15 s vs 87.06 s (pp. 11, 13); vs CPLEX 6.0 at matched quality (EPGAP = PE/100, 250 MB, 6,000 s, default and tuned settings): target reached on 44-45 of 120 instances, 565.84/592.19 s vs 7.52 s, and PE 3.94/2.35 vs 0.93 at the limit (pp. 13, 15); ADP-P and ADP-N need sample-size tuning and are not competitive (pp. 10-11, 15).
positioning: ADP literature reviewed as a toolkit (Bellman, Bertsekas-Tsitsiklis, look-ahead schemes of Sarkar et al. and Bertsimas-Teo-Vohra) (p. 2); MKP heuristics grouped into greedy, aggregation, tabu and genetic, exact methods dismissed in one clause (p. 3); the Chu-Beasley GA chosen as the strongest rival (pp. 3, 11); predecessors judged by numbers only.
writing: Abstract lists four findings (a)-(d), the last negative (p. 1); objective stated as a question (p. 2); five numbered evaluation questions (p. 9); three numbered conclusions including a serendipitous and a negative one (p. 15); hedged register (pp. 1, 15).
limits_future: No guarantees; the GA is better on quality (p. 13); ADP-P and ADP-N need tuning and are not competitive (pp. 11, 15); sizes up to n = 1000; next step: ADP for generic binary IP (Bertsimas and Demir 2001, p. 15).

method_links.note: The protocol exists in heuristic form in 2002: incumbent heuristic as the starting solution, an LP bound instead of an MIO certificate, and a duel with literature heuristics, the Chu-Beasley GA and CPLEX 6.0 (default and tuned) with machine, limits and speed normalization stated; here the heuristic wins and the exact solver loses. Also card-level evidence for Heuristic 4 (negative result printed in abstract and conclusions) and Tension T2 (a heuristic engine as the product).

Pre-speed-up data point: in his own matched-quality test CPLEX 6.0 needs about 75 times as long as ADP-H2 and on most instances does not reach its quality within 6,000 s, the belief Method 2 later concedes was right when formed.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: EPGAP set to the heuristic's achieved LP gap, 250 MB and 6,000 s limits, default and tuned CPLEX settings, time-to-quality and quality-at-limit both reported
base-heuristic value scaled by the truncated LP bound as cost-to-go; also S034's LP-relaxation value function

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: bound-referenced quality yardstick for heuristics and policies

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: asymptotic probabilistic analysis as a design prior

transferable: Matched-quality solver benchmark: set the MIP solver's gap tolerance to the heuristic's achieved bound gap, cap time and memory, run default and tuned settings, and report time-to-quality, quality-at-limit and the number of instances reaching the target (pp. 13-15).
In a two-branch look-ahead, scale both heuristic estimates to the same percentage gap below a common LP bound before comparing them (p. 4).
Adaptive LP fixing as a primal heuristic: fix variables at 1, zero those below delta, zero the least fractional and re-solve; delta trades time for quality and delta = 1 is plain truncation (p. 6).
Report heuristic quality as % deviation from the LP bound so every table entry is also an upper bound on the optimality gap (p. 9).
Define algorithmic robustness as the spread of time and quality across same-size instances and report min/avg/max (pp. 9-10, 14).
Rescale a rival's published times by a stated machine-speed ratio, and publish your own instances (pp. 9, 11).

quotes.text: the ADP approach based on parametric and nonparametric approximations, while producing reasonable solutions, is not competitive.
Although not the main focus of the paper the adaptive fixing heuristic for the MKP was surprisingly strong. It is fast and accurate.

title: Robust discrete optimization and network flows
contribution: Extends the budgeted (Γ) uncertainty model to discrete optimization: the robust MIP stays a MIP of moderately larger size, 0-1 problems with cost uncertainty are solved by n + 1 nominal problems so polynomial solvability and α-approximability carry over, and robust min-cost flow reduces to a logarithmic number of nominal flows on a modified network (pp. 1-15).
problem_entry: RO+IO (LO for flows): stochastic programming needs distributions rarely known and suffers scenario blow-up (p. 1); Soyster is over-conservative, ellipsoidal counterparts are conic and not directly applicable to discrete problems, and Kouvelis-Yu or minimax-regret robustness make polynomial problems NP-hard (p. 2); goal: tunable conservatism and tractability 'both practically and theoretically' (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Dualize the budgeted adversary: the robust MIP stays a MIP (Theorem 1, pp. 5-6); for 0-1 cost uncertainty a threshold θ makes the objective piecewise linear with breakpoints at the d_j, so n + 1 (or f + 1) nominal solves suffice (Theorem 3, Algorithm A, pp. 8-10); α-approximations transfer (Theorem 4, pp. 10-11); robust min-cost flow via an arc-splitting gadget and binary search over θ (Theorems 5-7, pp. 12-15).
assumptions: Model U: independent, symmetric, bounded constraint coefficients with unknown distribution, costs in [c_j, c_j + d_j] (pp. 3-4); Γ_i fractional, Γ_0 integer (p. 4); 0-1 variables critical for Theorem 3 (p. 10); no probabilistic assumption on costs, hence no suboptimality claims (p. 7); finite arc capacities without loss of generality (p. 13).
proof_devices: Inner maximum as an LP over z in [0,1] with sum z <= Γ, then strong duality; counterpart size 2n + m + l (Theorem 1, pp. 5-6)
Violation bound imported from S001, independent of x* (Theorem 2 and remarks, pp. 6-7)
Threshold dualization with the 0-1 identity max(d_j x_j - θ, 0) = max(d_j - θ, 0) x_j and interval decomposition of θ with endpoint optimality (Theorem 3, pp. 8-9)
Approximation transfer Z_B <= α(G_l - d_l) + d_l <= αG_l, with a TSP triangle-inequality counter-remark (Theorem 4, p. 11)
Four-arc gadget turning the positive part into a min-cost flow (Theorem 5, Fig. 1, pp. 12-13)
Convexity of Z(θ) and an |A|-Lipschitz bound via Lagrangian duality (Theorem 6, pp. 14-15)
Binary search with 2 ceil(log2(|A|θ̄/ε)) + 3 flow solves (Theorem 7, p. 15); as extracted, the proof gives an additive error ε while the statement is relative (1 + ε) [reader's note]
experiments: Robust knapsack n = 200 with CPLEX 7.0 on a Pentium II 400 PC, 0.05-50 s: Γ = 36.8 gives a 5.71e-3 bound for a 1.54% loss, full protection costs 5.5%, and over 20 instances a 2% loss brings the bound below 1e-3 (pp. 16-17; S001 reports the same run as CPLEX 6.0); robust sorting: Algorithm A finds all Γ in under a second vs CPLEX 7.0 at 30-80 min per Γ, and simulated cost jumps (p = 0.2, 20,000 samples) show σ down 32.1% for +20.37% nominal cost with CDF dominance (pp. 18-19); robust shortest path on 300 nodes and 1,475 arcs, Dijkstra |A| + 1 times, non-dominated Γ left to risk preference (p. 22); no comparison with Kouvelis-Yu or minimax regret; no failure case.
positioning: Placed against stochastic programming, Soyster, Ben-Tal-Nemirovski and El Ghaoui, Kouvelis-Yu, minimax regret and Averbakh (pp. 1-2); credits its own working paper [7] for the LP approach and Theorem 2 (pp. 2, 6); claims a unique position: it retains complexity or approximability unlike all other approaches (p. 22).
writing: Contribution-list abstract with the complexity results as headline (p. 1), contributions repeated (pp. 2-3); 'surprisingly' before the polynomiality result (p. 7); each theorem followed by a Remark marking where it breaks (pp. 10, 11, 13); hedged 'We feel' conclusion (p. 22); paragraphs shared nearly verbatim with S001 (pp. 4, 16-17).
limits_future: 0-1 requirement (p. 10); approximation transfer requires modified instances to stay in the approximable subclass (p. 11); no suboptimality claims under cost uncertainty (p. 7); parametric method not polynomial (p. 13); no future work beyond practical usefulness (p. 22).

method_links.note: Source of step 3's n + 1 nominal solves: the robust MIP stays a MIP, cost-robust 0-1 problems keep polynomial solvability and α-approximability, and robust min-cost flow stays a sequence of flows; boundaries printed.

On its Limitations line: in 2003 'tractable' already pairs complexity class with measured time ('both practically and theoretically'; Algorithm A under a second vs CPLEX 30-80 min per Γ), so the 2004-2019 drift is one of emphasis, not meaning.

One Γ knob per constraint and for the objective, a solution-independent violation bound, price curves on knapsack, sorting and shortest path, the over-conservative end shown and a non-dominated case left to risk preference; no bad case like PILOT4.
The duel is a structure-exploiting algorithm against a general MIP solver on the same robust model, not a warm-started MIO against a heuristic.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: robust solutions evaluated under cost jumps with probability p over 20,000 samples, with σ and CDF dominance; also S001 p. 12 and S034 pp. 17-19

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: oracle reduction transferring complexity and approximability
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: robust problem solved by a counted number of nominal-solver calls (n + 1, f + 1, or a logarithmic number of flows)

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: staged companion papers from one model
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: cites S001 as a 2001 working paper and shares paragraphs with it; S019 later restates both as norms

transferable: Budgeted-cost robustness for 0-1 problems: dualize the adversary to a threshold θ, use max(d_j x_j - θ, 0) = max(d_j - θ, 0) x_j, solve one nominal problem per breakpoint, and count only distinct d_j values (pp. 8-10).
When transferring an approximation guarantee through modified instances, check that they stay in the approximable subclass, as with the triangle inequality for TSP (p. 11).
Arc-splitting gadget: a capacity-θ/d branch at cost 0 plus an overflow branch at cost d models max(x - θ/d, 0) inside a network flow (pp. 12-13).
For a one-parameter family of nominal problems, prove convexity and a Lipschitz constant, then binary search with the number of nominal solves stated as a function of ε (pp. 14-15).

Evaluate robust solutions under a perturbation model other than the design set (20,000 samples, standard deviation, CDF dominance), and say when a non-dominated knob value is left to the user's risk preference (pp. 18-22).

quotes.text: We next show that surprisingly, the robust counterpart of a polynomially solvable combinatorial optimization problem is also polynomially solvable.
Unlike all other approaches that create robust solutions for combinatorial optimization problems, the proposed approach retains the complexity of the nominal problem or its approximability guarantee

title: Revenue management in a dynamic network environment
contribution: Proposes certainty equivalent control for network revenue management, pricing each request by the difference of two LP-relaxation values (unique and non-additive), proves its structural relation to the industry's additive bid prices, extends it to cancellations and overbooking, and shows in simulation that it is near-optimal and more robust to forecast error than bid-price control (pp. 2-21).
problem_entry: SD+LO+AP: enters through industry practice: revenue management's documented impact (p. 2) and two named defects of the widely used additive bid prices, non-uniqueness under multiple dual solutions and blindness to basis changes from group and multileg requests (p. 4); accept or reject requests to maximize expected revenue (pp. 2-3).
key_idea: Approximate the DP value by the LP relaxation and set the opportunity cost of request j to LP(n, D) - LP(n - A_j, D) (p. 8); a generic MP-policy for any value-approximating program (pp. 8-9); rollout, Monte Carlo demand sampling and overbooking via oversale variables with adjusted revenues and capacities (pp. 9, 13-14); network-flow form for OD and linear networks (p. 8).
assumptions: At most one request per period (p. 3); demand independent of the control policy, admitted as a simplification (p. 3); independent demands (p. 6); unbiased expected-demand forecasts (p. 7); cancellation and no-show probabilities independent of booking time and no goodwill effects (p. 13); synthetic networks N2-N4.2 under homogeneous and non-homogeneous Poisson demand (pp. 14-15).
proof_devices: DP <= perfect-hindsight value <= LP via Jensen on the concave LP value (Proposition 1, p. 7; full proof in Popescu 1999)
Network-flow integrality for OD fares (Proposition 2, p. 8)
Sandwich BP_j(n) <= OC_LP_j <= BP_j(n - A_j) by evaluating each LP at the other's optimal dual solution (Proposition 3, p. 10)
Acceptance structure from complementary and strict complementary slackness (Propositions 4-5, Table 1, pp. 10-11)
Four-node hub example realizing four cases, including a counterexample to decreasing differences (pp. 11-12)
Asymptotic optimality in the Talluri-van Ryzin fluid scaling 'by imitating their proof' (pp. 9-10)
Dual bound on forecast bias E[LP(n, D + eps)] - LP(n, D) <= (R - v'A)^+ E[eps] (p. 17)
Overbooking extensions of Proposition 1 and Section 4 asserted without proof (p. 14)
experiments: Exact expected values on two-leg networks (exact DP about two hours at 50 seats per leg and T = 300, p. 15); simulations on common random numbers in MATLAB 4.0 on a 450 MHz Celeron with NT = 100 trials (pp. 14, 17); C on a Pentium III for overbooking (p. 19); LP and perfect-information upper bounds (p. 21); CEC near-optimal at long horizons while BPC is off by a constant (p. 16); up to 2% better on larger networks (p. 17); CEC more robust to biased and noisy forecasts (pp. 17-19); rollout about +10% for BPC (p. 18); Monte Carlo poor with 30 or fewer trials (p. 18); BPC better at cancellation probability 0.30 (p. 19); BPC dual choice not enforced in the authors' code (p. 16); reader's notes: text claims do not match extracted Tables 4, 8 and 9 (pp. 17-21).
positioning: Reviews single-leg RM, threshold-time results, bid prices (Simpson, Williamson) and dynamic network models (Talluri-van Ryzin, Chen et al., Gunther et al.), none with cancellations (pp. 5-6); candid credit: Bitran-Mondschein proposed a similar LP heuristic without analysis, the LP is Williamson's, the network flow that of Glover et al. and Chen (p. 6); rollout from Bertsekas-Tsitsiklis (p. 9).
writing: Numbered contributions with headline numbers (pp. 4-5); a structure paragraph and a notation section (pp. 4-5); one worked example reused as a test network (pp. 11, 14-15); 'Interestingly' and 'Surprisingly' (pp. 5, 12); bullet conclusions defining 'robust' in three senses (pp. 20-21); one open idea stated twice (pp. 9, 18).
limits_future: Policy-independent demand (p. 3); no goodwill effects (p. 13); small instances (p. 14); unclear regime near load factor one (p. 20); BPC wins at a high cancellation rate (p. 19); rollout values costly to compute and store (p. 18); future: which preprocessing simulations to store for rollout (pp. 9, 18).

method_links.note: The baseline is the industry's current rule (the widely used bid-price control) and policies are scored by expected revenue with running times reported; but demand is synthetic and there are no owner's data.

The dynamic stochastic problem is approximated within LP (a network flow for OD and linear networks); structure is read off the dual (Propositions 3-5); the boundary is printed (a CEC-suboptimal case; the threshold property fails in networks).
Duel with the incumbent policy on common random numbers, with exact DP values and LP and perfect-information upper bounds in place of certificates.

Weak: the paper draws on Popescu's 1999 thesis, which holds the full proofs; an earlier student's thesis on the same topic (Chi) appears only in the references (Heuristic 7, weak; student list from note 06). Also card-level evidence for Heuristic 4 (negative cases printed) and Tension T6 (text headlines vs extracted tables).

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: generic MP-policy: any program approximating the value function yields an opportunity-cost rule; CEC uses the LP relaxation; also S070

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: structural comparison theorem with the incumbent before simulation
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: the CEC opportunity cost sandwiched between bid prices at two states, plus an accept/reject table by primal structure
policies given biased and correlated-noise forecasts while the simulator uses true demand, with bias scaled by 1, 2 and 4; also S001 and S004

transferable: Opportunity cost as an LP-value difference, LP(n, D) - LP(n - A_j, D): unique where dual prices are not, and sensitive to bundle effects (p. 8).
A sandwich inequality against the incumbent's price from cross-evaluated dual solutions, plus an accept/reject table by primal structure (pp. 10-11).
One small example that realizes every qualitative case, including a counterexample to the structural property the field hoped would extend (pp. 11-12).
Simulation protocol: common random numbers, exact DP where computable, and LP and perfect-information upper bounds beside every simulated value (pp. 14, 16, 21).

Forecast-error robustness test: the policy sees biased or correlated-noise forecasts while the simulator uses the true demand, bias scaled by 1, 2 and 4, paired with a dual bound on how bias moves the LP value (p. 17).
Put cancellations and no-shows into the LP through adjusted revenues and capacities plus an explicit oversale variable, so overbooking becomes dynamic and implicit in admission control (pp. 13-14).

quotes.text: Capturing and quantifying this type of feedback phenomenon is a subtle task that goes beyond the scope of this work. We will thus make the simplifying assumption that the demand process is independent of the control policy.
We restricted our attention to smaller instances with the explicit objective to obtain insights into the behavior of both BPC and CEC.

title: The price of robustness
contribution: Introduces the budget-of-uncertainty robust LP, whose counterpart stays an LP (or MIP) with a per-constraint knob Γ_i, proves tight solution-independent violation bounds for symmetric data and a dual-based marginal price of protection, and maps the price of robustness on a knapsack, a portfolio and NetLib PILOT4, where it stays high (pp. 1-16).
problem_entry: RO+LO (IO in the knapsack, AP in the portfolio): Soyster's robust LP is too conservative, and the ellipsoidal counterparts of Ben-Tal-Nemirovski and El Ghaoui are nonlinear and unattractive for discrete problems (pp. 1-3); motivated by the rival's NetLib finding (p. 1); aim: decrease 'what we call the price of robustness' (p. 1).
key_idea: Protect each constraint against at most floor(Γ_i) coefficients at their bounds plus one partial deviation ('nature will be restricted'), interpolating between nominal (Γ = 0) and Soyster (Γ = |J_i|) (p. 3); the protection LP dualizes into an LP counterpart that preserves sparsity (Theorem 1, p. 4); deterministic plus probabilistic guarantees (p. 4); a factor model for correlated data (p. 9).
assumptions: Model U: symmetric bounded coefficients with unknown distribution, independent for the bounds (pp. 2, 5); objective made certain via an epigraph variable (p. 2); correlated model C with independent symmetric sources (p. 9); nondegeneracy for the sensitivity result (p. 9); data: a random knapsack, Ben-Tal-Nemirovski's 150-stock portfolio and NetLib PILOT4 with 2% perturbations (pp. 10, 12, 14).
proof_devices: LP duality of the protection function (Proposition 1, Theorem 1, pp. 3-4)
Exchange argument reducing violation to Pr(sum γ_ij η_ij >= Γ_i) with γ_ij <= 1 (Proposition 2, pp. 4-5)
Moment-generating-function bound exp(-Γ^2/2|J_i|) via Markov's inequality and symmetry (Theorem 2, p. 5)
Best possible binomial bound by induction on n, tight for symmetric ±1 variables (Theorem 3(a)-(b), appendix pp. 16-18)
Computable bound via Robbins' Stirling inequalities, and CLT and De Moivre-Laplace asymptotics (Theorem 3(c)-(d), pp. 5-6, 18)
Numerical comparison of four bounds and the Γ needed for 1% violation: 33.9 of 200 but 5 of 5 (Figs. 1-3, Table 1, pp. 6-8)
Worst- and average-case protection comparison with ellipsoids (n^{1/4} vs a constant), declared inconclusive (p. 8)
Marginal price dObjective/dΓ_i = -z*_i q*_i via the matrix inversion lemma (Theorem 4, p. 9)
Correlated-data bound asserted 'analogously', without proof (p. 9)
experiments: Knapsack N = 200 with CPLEX 6.0 on a Pentium II 400 PC in 0.05-50 s: a 0.57% bound for a 1.54% loss, Soyster -5.5% (pp. 10, 12); Ben-Tal-Nemirovski's portfolio: phase transitions in Γ, 10,000 simulations at the tight two-point distribution with the bound close to the empirical frequency, minimum return above 12% from Γ = 15 (pp. 12, 14); PILOT4 (411 x 1,000, at most 29 uncertain coefficients per row): +3.68% even at violation probability 0.5 and +7.11% at full protection, diagnosed by the few uncertain coefficients per row (pp. 14, 16); no computational comparison with the ellipsoidal counterpart; the solver version differs from S004's report of the same knapsack.
positioning: Soyster as the Γ = |J_i| endpoint and Ben-Tal-Nemirovski and El Ghaoui as the ellipsoidal rival (pp. 1-3); claims to be 'at least as flexible ... and possibly more' (p. 2) though its own comparison ends inconclusive (p. 8); uses the rival's portfolio and NetLib cases (pp. 12, 14); novelty claimed 'To the best of our knowledge' (pp. 2, 10).
writing: Abstract runs history, concern and coined term (p. 1); key insights enumerated (pp. 10, 14-16); calibrated hedges ('some insight, but not conclusive evidence', 'admittedly unclear', 'We feel', pp. 6, 8, 16); a Remark discounts the paper's own first bound (p. 5).
limits_future: Symmetric, bounded, independent or factor-structured data (pp. 2, 9); poor value with few uncertain coefficients per row (pp. 14, 16); comparison with ellipsoids unresolved (p. 8); future: computation in real problems as the ultimate criterion (p. 8).

method_links.note: Source paper matching the SKILL steps: the property, one knob per constraint, solution-independent bounds, the class kept, curves on the rival's test problems and NetLib, and the PILOT4 bad case printed and diagnosed; extension: a marginal price by LP sensitivity.
The robust LP stays an LP that preserves sparsity; the robust MIP stays a MIP solvable like the nominal; sizes compared with the SOCP counterpart.
The duel is only with Soyster (the Γ = |J_i| endpoint) in every experiment; the ellipsoidal incumbent is compared analytically and inconclusively, never computationally.

[stated-joint] Computation is named the ultimate criterion, and NP-hard knapsacks of moderate size are 'often solved to optimality' by MIP solvers: measured tractability without a speed-up figure. Also card-level evidence for Heuristic 4 (PILOT4 printed).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: bound ladder with an operational table
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: simple, tight, computable and asymptotic bounds compared in figures, then Table 1 of the Γ needed for 1% violation by |J_i|
10,000 portfolio simulations under the tight two-point distribution, bound vs empirical frequency; also S004 and S034

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: marginal price of protection via LP sensitivity
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: derivative of the objective in Γ_i equals -z*_i q*_i under nondegeneracy

transferable: A fractional budget (floor(Γ) full deviations plus one partial) makes the robustness knob continuous while the inner problem stays an LP with a closed-form optimum (pp. 3-4).

Bound ladder: Chernoff-type, then tight combinatorial, then a computable Stirling-based bound, then the asymptotic; compare them in figures and tabulate the knob needed for 1% violation by problem size (pp. 5-8).
Marginal price of protection: -z*_i q*_i from the optimal primal and dual of the counterpart (p. 9).
Check a probability bound by simulating the distribution that makes it tight and plotting bound vs observed violation frequency (p. 12).
Run the method on the rival school's own instances (portfolio, NetLib) and print where it does not pay, with the structural reason (pp. 12, 14, 16).
Model correlated uncertainty by a few independent sources loading on all coefficients of a row, and put the budget on sources rather than coefficients (p. 9).

quotes.text: Moreover, we think that the ultimate criterion for comparing the degree of conservatism of these methods will be computation in real problems.
We attribute this to the fact that there are very few uncertain coefficients in each constraint (Table 4), and thus probabilistic protection is quite close to deterministic protection.

title: Robust linear optimization under general norms
contribution: Characterizes the robust LP counterpart for any norm-ball uncertainty set through the dual norm, recovering the ellipsoidal SOCP and the budget LP (as the D-norm) as special cases, bounds the D-norm against the Euclidean norm, and gives violation guarantees under arbitrary dependence with known mean and covariance (pp. 1-7).
problem_entry: RO+CP (LO): a structural entry: under ellipsoids the counterpart's class escalates from LP to SOCP to SDP to NP-hard, early approaches are not easy to generalize and very conservative, while the budget approach stays an LP (p. 2); goal: characterize the counterpart for arbitrary norms with guarantees allowing arbitrary dependencies (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: For U = {A : ||M(vec A - vec Ā)|| <= Ω} each constraint becomes ā_i'x + Ω||M^{-1}x_i||* <= b_i (Theorem 2, p. 3); the Euclidean norm gives an SOCP and L1/L∞ give LPs (pp. 3-4); the budget set is the D-norm with dual max(||s||∞, ||s||1/p), recovering the LP of [7] (Proposition 2, pp. 4-5); proximity bounds to the Euclidean norm (Proposition 3, pp. 5-6).
assumptions: Norm-ball uncertainty around the nominal matrix with invertible M (p. 3); Theorem 1 for compact convex sets taken from Ben-Tal-Nemirovski's lectures (pp. 2-3); for guarantees: an arbitrary unknown distribution with known mean and covariance, arbitrary dependencies, M = Σ^{-1/2} (p. 6); no data.
proof_devices: Support function of a compact convex deviation set (Theorem 1, p. 3)
Change of variables to the unit ball and the definition of the dual norm (Theorem 2, p. 3)
Dual of the D-norm by LP duality applied twice (Proposition 2, p. 4)
Norm proximity: convex maximization over a polytope at its extreme points, minimization by KKT (Proposition 3, pp. 5-6)
Bertsimas-Popescu one-sided multivariate Chebyshev bound P(X in S) <= 1/(1 + d^2) with d^2 from a KKT Mahalanobis projection (Theorem 3, p. 6)
experiments: none (n/a: a theory letter without computations)
positioning: Soyster and Falk as early conservative work (pp. 1-2); Ben-Tal-Nemirovski and El Ghaoui as the revival, with class escalation (p. 2); his own budget LP [7] (p. 2); presented as a unified treatment of [1,2,7,9,10] (p. 5); concedes that [7] has stronger bounds under independence and symmetry (p. 6).
writing: Seven-page letter; framing 'emerging as a leading methodology' (p. 1) and 'shed some new light' (p. 2); theorem-proof throughout; no conclusions section, ending on the weaker-but-wider trade-off (pp. 6-7).
limits_future: Bounds weaker than those of [7] when independence and symmetry hold (pp. 6-7); no computations; no future directions stated.

method_links.note: The class of the robust counterpart is read off the dual norm and the budget LP is recovered as a special case: 'read structure off the dual' in its plainest form.
The guarantee becomes distribution-free given mean and covariance, weaker than [7]'s but valid under dependence; no price curve and no bad case.
